meta.blurb: A drill used twice is a waste, thinks Mira, and she imagines a street where neighbours lend each other tools. Her friend Kofi asks one hard question: what if nobody wants it? Mira learns to test the idea with small, cheap experiments.
meta.bible: Mira: a nurse in her thirties with a new idea, curious and determined. Kofi: her friend, a carpenter, blunt and kind. Mr Reyes: owner of a hardware shop on Alder Street. Lucas: a friend who writes software. Anya: a neighbour, the first person Mira interviews. Alder Street: where Mira lives. Toolshelf: the name of Mira's idea, a way for neighbours to borrow tools instead of buying them. All numbers and results in the story are imagined illustrations, not real data, and no currency is named. Key terms used in this book: guess, riskiest guess, interview, small test, real actions, change course, early users, small steps, fee, cost of finding a customer, word of mouth. Many new ventures close within a few years, and the book says so without giving exact figures. Voice: warm, practical, concrete and kind, never preachy. The final beat says this is general information and not financial advice. Dina: Mira's older sister, who keeps the accounts for a bakery, calm and exact. Tomas: a retired plumber three doors down, with a garage full of unused tools. Priya: a young woman who has just moved to Alder Street with almost nothing. Mrs Haddad: owner of the Haddad Cafe on Alder Street. Hana: owner of a small paint shop on Birch Road. Jonas: a man with a van who rents out big machines. Birch Road: the next street over, where Toolshelf is tried a second time. Mill Lane: a third street, with a bicycle shop. Ben: Anya's teenage son, good with his hands.
chapters: The Guess That Could Sink It
A Shelf at the Hardware Shop

beats.scene: Mira stands in a garage holding a new drill beside a box of tools
beats.summary: Mira buys a drill she will use twice and has an idea: neighbours could lend each other tools.

beats.scene: A long street of houses, each garage door open on shelves of tools
beats.summary: On Alder Street almost every house owns the same tools, and most of them sit unused.

beats.scene: Mira in nurse's uniform sits at a kitchen table after a night shift
beats.summary: Mira is a nurse who works long shifts and dreams of building something of her own.

beats.scene: An old man in his garage beside a wall of neatly hung tools
beats.summary: Tomas, a retired plumber, shows Mira a garage of tools he has barely touched in years.

beats.scene: Mira writing the name Toolshelf at the top of a notebook page
beats.summary: Mira gives her idea a name, Toolshelf, and writes it at the top of a fresh page.

beats.scene: Mira drawing a phone screen with a map and tool icons
beats.summary: Mira imagines an app with a map where neighbours find and borrow tools.

beats.scene: Two sisters at a Sunday lunch table, one explaining with a notebook
beats.summary: Mira tells her sister Dina about Toolshelf, and Dina says it sounds lovely.

beats.scene: Mira at a table with bank papers and a calculator
beats.summary: Mira checks her savings and sees she could live for a year on them.

beats.scene: Mira asleep at a table among scattered drawings of phone screens
beats.summary: Mira stays up late sketching screens and cannot stop thinking about Toolshelf.

beats.scene: Mira at the door of a woodworking shop holding her notebook
beats.summary: In the morning Mira takes her notebook to show her friend Kofi.

beats.scene: Kofi planing a board while Mira opens her notebook on the bench
beats.summary: In his workshop Kofi listens to Mira's idea while he works.

beats.scene: Mira pointing to a list of app features in her notebook
beats.summary: Mira lists everything the app will do: maps, payments, ratings and photographs.

beats.scene: A wall calendar with twelve months marked in coloured pens
beats.summary: Mira plans to build the whole app in secret over twelve months before showing anyone.

beats.scene: Mira marking months on a wall calendar with a green pen
beats.summary: She divides the year into months of design, building, polishing and launch.

beats.scene: Mira covering her notebook with her hand while Kofi looks on
beats.summary: Mira wants to keep it secret because she fears someone will copy it or laugh.

beats.scene: Kofi puts down the notebook with a frown in his sawdusty workshop
beats.summary: Kofi reads the plan twice and tells her it is a big bet.

beats.scene: Mira standing with crossed arms, looking hurt, in front of the bench
beats.summary: Mira feels stung and asks whether Kofi thinks the idea is bad.

beats.scene: Kofi leaning on a workbench, gently shaking his head
beats.summary: Kofi says he does not know if it is a bad idea, and that is the point.

beats.scene: Kofi holding up one finger as Mira listens with narrowed eyes
beats.summary: Kofi asks the question Mira cannot answer: what if nobody wants it?

beats.scene: Mira walking home along Alder Street at dusk, notebook closed
beats.summary: Mira walks home unable to answer, and the question stays with her.

beats.scene: Mira reading on a laptop at a kitchen table late at night
beats.summary: Mira reads that many new ventures close within a few years, without exact figures.

beats.scene: A shop window with beautiful goods and an empty street outside
beats.summary: Many ventures fail not because they were built badly but because nobody wanted them.

beats.scene: Two sisters on a sofa, one telling a story with her hands
beats.summary: Dina tells a story about a customer who perfected a cake box nobody asked for.

beats.scene: A tall pile of unsold cake boxes in a cramped spare room
beats.summary: The cake box man finally launched and found that bakers already had boxes they liked.

beats.scene: Mira drawing a big cloud of question marks around her notebook idea
beats.summary: An idea is not a fact but a bundle of guesses that have not been checked.

beats.scene: Mira sticking notes headed fact and guess on a kitchen wall
beats.summary: Mira sorts what she really knows from what she merely hopes.

beats.scene: Dina pointing at a notebook page across a table, smiling kindly
beats.summary: Dina points out that feeling sure and being right are different things.

beats.scene: Mira looking at a closed notebook with a worried frown
beats.summary: Mira fears that testing might kill her idea, and Kofi says it is better to learn now.

beats.scene: Scales weighing a small notebook against coins and a clock
beats.summary: Mira counts what a wrong guess would cost her: time, savings and energy.

beats.scene: Mira tearing the year calendar from the wall in a bright kitchen
beats.summary: Mira takes down her year plan and decides to list her guesses instead.

beats.scene: A garage wall covered with small yellow notes and a marker pen
beats.summary: Mira covers the garage wall with sticky notes, one guess on each.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading neighbours own tools they rarely use
beats.summary: The first guess: neighbours own tools that they rarely use.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading they will lend their tools to others
beats.summary: The second guess: people who own tools will be willing to lend them.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading neighbours will borrow instead of buying
beats.summary: The third guess: other neighbours will borrow instead of buying.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading people will trust a stranger with their tools
beats.summary: The fourth guess: people will trust a stranger enough to lend a tool.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading borrowing will be easier than buying
beats.summary: The fifth guess: borrowing from a neighbour will be easier than going to a shop.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading neighbours will use a phone app for this
beats.summary: The sixth guess: people, including older neighbours, will use an app.

beats.scene: Kofi adding a note to the garage wall with a pencil behind his ear
beats.summary: Kofi adds guesses Mira missed, about remembering to return tools and finding time.

beats.scene: Mira counting yellow notes with a finger in a bright garage
beats.summary: Mira counts fourteen guesses on the wall.

beats.scene: Mira standing back with arms folded, facing a wall of yellow notes
beats.summary: Mira steps back and sees that her whole plan is built on untested guesses.

beats.scene: Kofi pointing to the wall of notes with a pencil
beats.summary: Kofi asks which of the fourteen guesses matters most.

beats.scene: Mira holding a single note up to the light of the garage door
beats.summary: Mira asks of each guess: if this were wrong, would the idea survive?

beats.scene: Mira moving yellow notes to a pile marked fixable
beats.summary: Some wrong guesses can be fixed, like the app or the shop's convenience.

beats.scene: Mira holding one note alone in the middle of the empty wall
beats.summary: Other guesses are fatal: if nobody lends, there is no Toolshelf at all.

beats.scene: A tall tower of wooden blocks with one block at the bottom marked
beats.summary: The riskiest guess is the one that would sink the idea if it were wrong.

beats.scene: Mira circling one yellow note with a thick red marker
beats.summary: Mira's riskiest guess is that people will lend their tools to strangers at all.

beats.scene: Mira on a phone call in the garage, shaking her head
beats.summary: Lucas calls to offer to build the app, and Mira says wait.

beats.scene: A circled yellow note placed alone at the top of a bare wall
beats.summary: Mira puts the riskiest note at the top of the wall and leaves the others for later.

beats.scene: A short staircase drawn on paper with the riskiest note on the first step
beats.summary: Testing the riskiest guess first saves time, even though easy guesses are tempting.

beats.scene: Mira writing a single question on a clean page in neat capitals
beats.summary: Mira writes the question she needs answered: will a person lend a tool to a neighbour?

beats.scene: Mira and Kofi drinking tea on a workshop bench, talking
beats.summary: The cheapest way to learn is to talk to people before building anything.

beats.scene: Mira holding a notebook in front of a doorway, looking uncertain
beats.summary: Mira worries about just asking people whether they like her idea.

beats.scene: A neighbour smiling and nodding while holding a cup of tea
beats.summary: Asking about the future gets pleasant but unreliable answers.

beats.scene: Mira writing questions in her notebook with the word past underlined
beats.summary: Good questions ask about what people did in the past, not what they might do.

beats.scene: Mira reading from a notebook while Kofi thinks with one hand on his chin
beats.summary: Mira drafts a question: tell me about the last time you needed a tool you didn't own.

beats.scene: A neighbour waving off thanks with a laugh at a front gate
beats.summary: Compliments cost nothing and teach nothing, so Mira must watch what people do.

beats.scene: Mira and Kofi sitting opposite each other at a workbench, practising
beats.summary: Mira practises an interview on Kofi, who answers too politely.

beats.scene: Mira writing three short follow-up questions on a card
beats.summary: Mira adds follow-up questions: what happened next, and what did you do instead?

beats.scene: A nurse listening with a notepad beside a hospital bed
beats.summary: Mira realises that listening and asking about what happened is a skill she already has.

beats.scene: A handwritten card with five short questions beside a pen
beats.summary: Mira writes five short questions on a card and plans to knock on ten doors.

beats.scene: Mira at a front door, Anya smiling and pointing to a ladder
beats.summary: Anya, the first neighbour Mira interviews, tells how she borrowed a ladder from her brother.

beats.scene: A broken cheap hammer lying on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Anya also tells how a cheap tool she bought broke on its first use.

beats.scene: Tomas in his garage holding an old pipe wrench, shaking his head
beats.summary: Tomas lends to family and friends but lost a wrench he once lent to a stranger.

beats.scene: Priya sitting on the floor of a bare flat beside unhung shelves
beats.summary: Priya, a new tenant with almost nothing, still has no drill and no shelves.

beats.scene: Mrs Haddad behind a café counter pointing at a tall stepladder
beats.summary: Mrs Haddad, who runs the café, hired a machine for one day when she needed it.

beats.scene: A young father in a doorway holding a baby and a screwdriver
beats.summary: A young father says he never has time to ask, so he buys cheap tools.

beats.scene: Mira writing quickly in a notebook on a low garden wall
beats.summary: Mira writes down exact words and stops herself from pitching Toolshelf.

beats.scene: A door closing on a man's face while Mira stands on the step
beats.summary: One neighbour has no time and shuts the door, which also teaches Mira something.

beats.scene: Mr Reyes behind the hardware shop counter beside a rack of drills
beats.summary: Mr Reyes says customers often ask whether he has a tool they can borrow.

beats.scene: Mira sitting on a low wall with a thick notebook at sunset
beats.summary: After the tenth door, Mira sits with ten stories and is surprised by what she heard.

beats.scene: Mira spreading notebook pages across a floor with coloured pens
beats.summary: Mira lays out her notes and marks what people actually did, not what they said.

beats.scene: Two neighbours passing a ladder over a fence between gardens
beats.summary: People borrow easily from family and friends.

beats.scene: A closed garage door with a handwritten sign reading private
beats.summary: Strangers almost never lend, and the one man who tried it lost his tool.

beats.scene: Mira frowning at a note with a large question mark beside it
beats.summary: Mira's riskiest guess now looks weak: people lend only to those they know.

beats.scene: A hand counting nine fingers beside a notebook page
beats.summary: Of the nine who talked, most had borrowed from people they knew, and none from strangers.

beats.scene: Mira pointing to a sentence underlined twice on a notebook page
beats.summary: The real problem is finding the right tool quickly and trusting the person who has it.

beats.scene: Mira connecting three notebook stories with a line of green ink
beats.summary: Anya's drive, Priya's shelves and Mrs Haddad's hired machine are all the same problem.

beats.scene: Kofi and Mira sitting on a bench, Kofi smiling and patting her shoulder
beats.summary: Mira is disappointed that her app is not the answer, but Kofi says this is good news.

beats.scene: Mira drawing a new sketch of neighbours and tools linked by arrows
beats.summary: Mira reframes Toolshelf as a way to know who has what and who can be trusted.

beats.scene: A new yellow note placed at the top of a wall of older notes
beats.summary: Mira writes a new riskiest guess and decides to test it by hand.

beats.scene: Kofi drawing a small circle around one note on a workshop wall
beats.summary: The smallest test is aimed at the riskiest guess, not a smaller version of everything.

beats.scene: Lucas on a video call pointing at a screen with rough app sketches
beats.summary: Lucas offers to build a lite app in a month, but Mira sees it is not a small test.

beats.scene: Mira at a table with a pen and three rough ideas on paper
beats.summary: Mira asks what is the cheapest thing that could answer her question.

beats.scene: A paper list of tools pinned to a corkboard with a phone number
beats.summary: The idea: a paper list of tools pinned up on one street, with a phone number to call.

beats.scene: Mira at a table writing a neat list of tools and names
beats.summary: Neighbours tell Mira which tools they can lend, and she arranges each handover.

beats.scene: Mira's phone on a kitchen table with a small notebook beside it
beats.summary: Mira will run the service by hand, even though it will not work for a thousand people.

beats.scene: Mira on the phone, writing notes during a call beside a window
beats.summary: By doing it by hand Mira will see every request and hear every worry.

beats.scene: Mira drawing a neat box around a map of Alder Street
beats.summary: Mira limits the test to Alder Street, two weeks, and loans of a few days.

beats.scene: Dina examining a sheet of paper with raised eyebrows at a table
beats.summary: Dina thinks the test is too small, and Mira says that is the point.

beats.scene: A one-page plan with three headings: guess, test and count
beats.summary: Mira writes the test on one page: the guess, the test, and what she will count.

beats.scene: Mira at a table with a pen above the blank heading count
beats.summary: Kofi explains why you must decide what success is before the test begins.

beats.scene: Kofi holding a wooden chair with a price tag beside a row of chairs
beats.summary: Kofi tells how he once made ten chairs and called selling three a success.

beats.scene: Mira and Dina at a table with a calculator and a notebook
beats.summary: Mira and Dina discuss what number would be a fair target, not too easy or too hard.

beats.scene: A hand handing over a drill from a garage to another hand
beats.summary: Success must be a real action, such as lending a tool, not a promise or sign-up.

beats.scene: A page with the target written in large letters and underlined twice
beats.summary: The target is that at least five of twenty households lend a tool within two weeks.

beats.scene: Mira signing a sheet of paper while Kofi watches with a pencil
beats.summary: Mira signs the target and gives a copy to Kofi so she cannot change it later.

beats.scene: Mira pencilling three arrows labelled carry on, change and stop
beats.summary: Mira also decides in advance what she will do if the test falls short.

beats.scene: A street map with twenty houses marked by small blue dots
beats.summary: Mira chooses twenty houses on Alder Street for the test.

beats.scene: Mira at a printer with warm sheets of paper in her hand
beats.summary: Mira writes a short plain leaflet and prints twenty copies.

beats.scene: Mira pushing a leaflet through a letterbox on a bright morning
beats.summary: Mira delivers leaflets to twenty homes and waits for the first replies.

beats.scene: A silent phone on a kitchen table beside a cold cup of tea
beats.summary: On the first day Mira's phone does not ring.

beats.scene: Mira answering her phone with a surprised smile at the door
beats.summary: The first call comes from Anya, who says it is a great idea.

beats.scene: Mira reading handwritten notes pushed under her front door
beats.summary: Over the next days notes and kind words arrive from neighbours.

beats.scene: Mira smiling at a pile of kind notes on her table
beats.summary: Mira is tempted to count all the kind words as a success.

beats.scene: A notebook page divided into two columns with tally marks
beats.summary: Mira keeps two columns: what people say and what people do.

beats.scene: Tomas at a front door holding a router and a tile cutter
beats.summary: On the fifth day Tomas phones to offer his router and a tile cutter.

beats.scene: Priya on a ladder fixing a shelf to the wall with a drill
beats.summary: Priya borrows a drill and hangs her shelves at last.

beats.scene: A phone lying silent on a table with a calendar showing day ten
beats.summary: In the second week the calls slow down and people say they will think about it.

beats.scene: A tally sheet showing fourteen ticks on the left and three on the right
beats.summary: At the end fourteen people said they wanted to join, but only three offered a tool.

beats.scene: Mira holding two sheets of paper side by side at a table
beats.summary: Three of twenty is below the written target of five, so there is nothing to argue about.

beats.scene: Mira writing a short sentence at the top of a clean notebook page
beats.summary: Mira writes down the lesson: words and actions differ, and many say yes but few do.

beats.scene: A glittering banner reading fourteen sign-ups above an empty shelf
beats.summary: Fourteen sign-ups look impressive, but big flattering numbers can hide what is really happening.

beats.scene: Dina tapping a column of figures with a pencil in a bakery office
beats.summary: Dina says a number that cannot be wrong is dangerous, so ask what people did.

beats.scene: Mira holding a list of names and a phone, thinking
beats.summary: Mira decides to call the people who said yes but did not lend, to ask them why.

beats.scene: A man at his front door holding a power saw protectively
beats.summary: A neighbour at number twelve fears that his tools would be damaged.

beats.scene: A woman in a doorway shrugging beside an empty hook on the wall
beats.summary: A woman says she once lent a ladder and never got it back.

beats.scene: A tired man at a kitchen table with a phone and a clock
beats.summary: Others say the handover is too much effort for busy people.

beats.scene: Anya on her doorstep with her hands raised in a rueful shrug
beats.summary: Anya admits she said yes only because Mira was so nice at her door.

beats.scene: Mira sorting reasons into four coloured piles on a table
beats.summary: Mira groups the reasons: fear of damage, fear of loss, effort, and not knowing the borrower.

beats.scene: Mira circling the word Tomas next to the word Mira on a page
beats.summary: Mira sees that the three lenders trusted a person they knew, namely Mira herself.

beats.scene: Mira and Kofi at a bench with three arrows drawn on a board
beats.summary: After a test there are three choices: carry on, change course, or stop.

beats.scene: Mira shaking her head in front of a sheet marked carry on
beats.summary: Carrying on unchanged would be stubbornness, because the evidence was weak.

beats.scene: Mira studying three notebook pages about Priya, Anya and Mrs Haddad
beats.summary: Stopping would also be too hasty, because the need she found was real.

beats.scene: Mira at a window looking down Alder Street at dusk
beats.summary: Mira asks whom the people on Alder Street already trust.

beats.scene: Mr Reyes's shop window with tools and a friendly hand-painted sign
beats.summary: Mira thinks of Mr Reyes, whom everyone trusts and who is asked about lending every week.

beats.scene: A wooden shelf in a shop with a row of labelled tools
beats.summary: The change: tools will sit on a shelf in a trusted shop instead of in neighbours' garages.

beats.scene: Mira checking off four reasons beside a drawing of a shop shelf
beats.summary: The shop answers the four fears: damage, loss, effort and the unknown borrower.

beats.scene: Kofi leaning on a doorway, asking a question with a raised eyebrow
beats.summary: Kofi asks whether the failed test was a waste, and Mira counts what it cost.

beats.scene: A tiny pile and a tall pile of coins on a table
beats.summary: The test taught her more than a year of planning would have, at a tiny cost.

beats.scene: Mira writing missed and learned on the signed target page
beats.summary: Mira writes missed but learned on her target page and feels lighter.

beats.scene: Mira talking to Mr Reyes across the counter before opening time
beats.summary: Mira visits Mr Reyes early and tells him what she has learned.

beats.scene: Mr Reyes frowning as he folds his arms behind a till
beats.summary: Mr Reyes worries that lending tools will cost him sales and tools.

beats.scene: Mira and Mr Reyes looking at a shelf in a corner of the shop
beats.summary: Mira offers a small, low-risk trial with her own tools and her own responsibility for losses.

beats.scene: Mr Reyes shaking Mira's hand across the shop counter
beats.summary: Mr Reyes agrees to try a shelf of borrowable tools for one month.

beats.scene: Mira writing a sentence at the top of a new notebook page
beats.summary: Mira writes the new guess: people will borrow from a trusted shop and bring tools back.

beats.scene: Mira and Dina signing a page headed target at a kitchen table
beats.summary: Mira writes the new target in advance: at least ten loans, most tools returned, and repeat visitors.

beats.scene: Neighbours carrying drills and ladders into a small hardware shop
beats.summary: Neighbours donate twelve tools, including Tomas's router and Kofi's clamps.

beats.scene: Kofi screwing a pine shelf to the wall with a drill
beats.summary: Kofi builds a simple pine shelf, and each tool gets a label.

beats.scene: A small paper book and a pen tied by string to the shelf
beats.summary: Mira runs the second test by hand with a paper sign-out book.

beats.scene: Mira behind a counter with a sign above the new shelf
beats.summary: On opening day Mira stands in the shop at lunchtime, waiting for the first borrower.

beats.scene: A teenage boy signing the paper book beside the tool shelf
beats.summary: The first borrower is Ben, Anya's teenage son, who needs a spirit level.

beats.scene: Mira ticking two lines in the paper book at closing time
beats.summary: By closing time two tools have been lent, and Mira writes them down.

beats.scene: Mira's notebook with a chart of seven pencilled bars for the week
beats.summary: In the first week seven tools are lent, to people she did not expect.

beats.scene: Mira sorting names in a notebook into three small groups
beats.summary: Mira looks for the people who need the service most: new tenants, new parents and weekend hobbyists.

beats.scene: A father in the shop holding a drill beside a baby gate
beats.summary: A new father borrows a drill to fit a baby gate and says he would never have asked a neighbour.

beats.scene: A man in the shop carrying a jigsaw and a bird box plan
beats.summary: A weekend hobbyist borrows a jigsaw to build a bird box.

beats.scene: Mira circling a name that appears three times in the paper book
beats.summary: Mira watches who comes back, because repeat visits are the clearest sign of usefulness.

beats.scene: Priya in the shop with a friend, pointing to the tool shelf
beats.summary: Priya comes back for a second tool and brings a friend.

beats.scene: Mr Reyes ringing up screws and paint for a customer holding a drill
beats.summary: Mr Reyes notices that borrowers also buy screws, paint and sandpaper from him.

beats.scene: A tally sheet with fourteen loans and four repeat names starred
beats.summary: After two weeks there are fourteen loans and four repeat borrowers, both reaching the target.

beats.scene: Mr Reyes and Mira reading a tally sheet across the shop counter
beats.summary: At the end of the month the target is met, and Mr Reyes asks to carry on.

beats.scene: Mira's notebook showing a sketch of five shops and a delivery van
beats.summary: Mira is tempted to launch big, with more shops, a van and a website.

beats.scene: Kofi at his bench shaking his head and pointing at a joint
beats.summary: Kofi tells her that small steps beat big launches: try a little and adjust.

beats.scene: Kofi tapping a half-built wooden cupboard with a pencil
beats.summary: Kofi explains that he never builds a whole cupboard before checking the first joint.

beats.scene: Mira writing four words in large letters on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: Mira sets a weekly rhythm: choose a guess, run a small test, count, and decide.

beats.scene: Mira taping a label reading hang a shelf onto a tool
beats.summary: Her first weekly guess is that tools labelled by job will be borrowed more than tools labelled by name.

beats.scene: A tally with a small bar rising next to relabelled tools
beats.summary: After a week with job labels, loans of the relabelled tools rise from three to five.

beats.scene: Mira pinning a long row of weekly sheets along a kitchen wall
beats.summary: What matters is the speed of learning, not the speed of building.

beats.scene: Mira and a small money box on a table beside a calculator
beats.summary: Mira sets a limited budget and finds that spending slowly makes her think more clearly.

beats.scene: A hand putting a coin back into a small jar
beats.summary: A small budget makes Mira ask whether there is a cheaper way to learn each thing.

beats.scene: Mira and Mr Reyes looking at a sign beside the free tool shelf
beats.summary: A polite yes is easy but a payment is real, so Mira wants to know if people will pay.

beats.scene: A yellow note reading people will pay a small fee to borrow
beats.summary: She writes a new guess: people will pay a small fee to borrow a tool.

beats.scene: Mira looking at a poster with a price drawn in thick letters
beats.summary: She decides not to ask whether people would pay, but to charge a small fee and watch.

beats.scene: Kofi and Mira bent over a sheet with three prices crossed out
beats.summary: Kofi says the fee must be small but real, so it carries meaning.

beats.scene: A signed page headed target lying beside a small cash tin
beats.summary: Mira writes the target first: at least six of ten borrowers keep borrowing at the new price.

beats.scene: A small sign beside the tool shelf explaining the new fee
beats.summary: A small honest sign explains that the fee keeps the tools in good repair.

beats.scene: A customer smiling and handing a coin to Mira beside the shelf
beats.summary: Borrowers react differently: one grumbles, one asks questions, one pays happily.

beats.scene: A tally sheet with eight ticks and two crosses beside a cash tin
beats.summary: Of ten borrowers offered the fee, eight still borrow, so people will pay.

beats.scene: Mira on the phone taking notes beside an open paper book
beats.summary: Mira asks the two who stopped, and learns the fee was too high for very short jobs.

beats.scene: Mira writing a careful note about small numbers on a pad
beats.summary: Eight payments are worth more than fourteen compliments, but ten borrowers is still a small number.

beats.scene: Dina and Mira at a bakery table with a pad of figures
beats.summary: Dina asks what each new borrower costs Mira to find.

beats.scene: Mira dividing a column of costs by a column of names
beats.summary: Mira divides her spending by the number of new borrowers: the cost of finding a customer.

beats.scene: A small cash tin with coins stacked in neat columns

B1B2: Mira has just bought a drill for one small job, and it will probably stay in a box for years. She has an idea: what if neighbours could lend each other tools instead?
Mira lives on Alder Street, a quiet road of small houses with garages. Almost every garage holds the same things: a drill, a ladder, a saw and a lawn mower.
Mira works as a nurse, and her shifts often last twelve hours. She loves the job, but lately she has been wondering what it would feel like to build something of her own.
Tomas, a retired plumber, waves her into his garage and shows her shelf after shelf of tools. He admits that he has not touched most of them since he stopped working.
That evening she opens a new notebook and thinks of a name for her idea. She writes Toolshelf in large letters at the top of the first page.
Mira sketches a phone screen with a map of the street. On the map, little tool icons show who owns what, and one tap would send a request.
On Sunday, Mira shows her sister Dina the notebook over lunch. Dina, who keeps the accounts for a bakery, smiles and says that it sounds lovely.
Later that week, Mira sits down and counts her savings very carefully. If she worked fewer hours at the hospital, she could live on them for about a year.
That night Mira cannot sleep at all, so she sits down at the table. She fills six pages with drawings of screens, buttons and menus, and by the time she stops, the sky outside is turning grey.
In the morning, still full of energy, Mira walks to the workshop of her friend Kofi. She is sure he will love the idea as much as she does.
Kofi is planing a long board when Mira arrives, and he keeps working while she talks. He nods now and then, but he does not smile yet.
Mira reads out her list of features: maps, payments, ratings, photographs and reminders. The list is so long that it runs onto a second page.
Mira decides to build a complete app with maps, payments and ratings. She will keep it secret for a year, and then she will surprise everyone with the finished product.
She divides the year into clear stages, with a plan for each month. Three months are for drawing, six for building and testing, two for polishing, and one for the big launch.
Kofi asks why the plan has to be secret. Mira says she is afraid that someone might copy it, or that people might laugh at an unfinished idea.
Kofi, a carpenter and an old friend, reads the plan and frowns. He says that a year is a long time to work on something that nobody has asked for yet.
Mira feels stung, because she had hoped for praise. She asks him if he thinks the idea is bad, and her voice is sharper than she intended.
Kofi shakes his head and says that he does not know whether it is bad. He adds, gently, that Mira does not know either, and that this is exactly the problem.
Then Kofi asks the question that Mira has been avoiding without knowing it. What will she do if she builds everything and nobody wants to use it?
Mira walks home slowly in the evening light, feeling uneasy. She cannot answer Kofi's question, and it follows her all the way to her front door.
That night Mira reads about new ventures online for a long time. She learns that many of them close within a few years, although the exact numbers differ from place to place and from year to year.
The more she reads, the more one reason stands out. Many ventures fail not because they were built badly, but because nobody wanted what they made.
When Mira calls her, Dina tells a story about a customer at the bakery. He spent two years designing a perfect cake box, and he never asked a single baker what they needed.
When he finally showed his box to the bakers, they were polite, but they already had boxes they liked. He sold almost none, and a spare room filled with unsold boxes.
Slowly Mira starts to understand something very important about her idea. An idea feels like a fact when you are excited, but it is really a bundle of guesses that nobody has checked yet.
Mira writes two headings on a page: things I know, and things I hope. The first column is almost empty, while the second runs on and on.
Dina visits the next day and reads the two columns. She says kindly that feeling sure and being right are cousins, but they are not the same person.
Mira admits to Kofi, a little ashamed, that she is afraid. If she tests the idea, it might fail, and then she will have nothing left.
She writes down what a wrong guess could cost. It would take a year of her time, most of her savings, and a great deal of her energy.
Mira takes the year calendar down from the wall and folds it away. She decides that her first step is not to build, but to write down her guesses.
On Saturday morning Mira clears a space on her garage wall. She will write each guess behind Toolshelf on its own yellow note.
Her first note reads: neighbours own tools that they rarely use. She thinks of Tomas and his silent wrenches, and she decides that this one is probably true.
The second note is much harder to write than the first one. Owning tools is one thing, but will people really lend them to others, even for a few days?
The third guess is that people who need a tool will choose to borrow it. They might prefer to buy their own, or to ask a friend.
The fourth guess is about trust, and it matters most. Would a person hand a good saw to someone they have never met, and expect to see it again?
The fifth guess is that borrowing from a neighbour will be easier than buying at a shop. But the hardware shop on Alder Street is only five minutes away.
The sixth guess is about the app itself and who will use it. Mira realises that Tomas does not own a smartphone, and that many neighbours might never download it.
Kofi comes to the garage and reads the wall. He adds two notes of his own: people will remember to return things, and people will find time to meet.
Mira counts the notes on the wall, and there are fourteen of them. She had expected five or six, and she is a little shocked.
Mira steps back and looks at the whole wall for a while. Her beautiful plan is standing on fourteen small guesses, and she has not checked a single one.
Kofi looks along the wall and asks Mira which of the fourteen notes matters most. She starts to say that they all do, and then she stops.
Kofi gives her a simple question to ask about each note. If this guess turned out to be wrong, would the idea still survive?
Some of the notes turn out to be fixable. If people dislike the app, she could use paper or the telephone, and if the shop is close, she could lend other tools.
A few of the notes are quite different from the rest. If nobody is willing to lend a tool, there is nothing to borrow, and no clever app in the world can fix that.
Kofi tells her that not all guesses matter equally. The riskiest guess is the one that would sink the whole idea if it turned out to be wrong.
Mira thinks about it very carefully for a long time. Her most dangerous guess is that people will lend their own tools to near strangers at all, and everything else depends on it.
Lucas, a friend who writes software, calls to offer his help. Mira thanks him warmly, but she tells him that it is too early, and that she needs to learn something first.
Mira moves the circled note to the top of the wall and leaves the rest lower down. Those other guesses can wait, because they matter only if this one is true.
Mira understands exactly why the order of the tests really matters. It would be easy to start with the simple guesses, but then she might spend months learning the wrong things.
Mira writes one clear question on a clean page: will a person lend a tool to a neighbour they barely know? She decides to find the answer before she builds anything.
Kofi tells her that the cheapest way to learn is simply to talk to people. It costs no money, it needs no software, and she can start tomorrow.
Mira asks Kofi whether she should simply describe Toolshelf and ask neighbours if they like it. Kofi winces and tells her that this is exactly the wrong thing to do.
Kofi explains that questions about the future, like would you lend a tool, get cheerful answers. People mean them when they say them, but they often do not follow through.
Good questions, says Kofi, ask about what people actually did in the past. Instead of asking what someone might do, you ask what they really did last time.
Mira drafts her first question: tell me about the last time you needed a tool you did not own. What did you do, and how did that go?
Kofi also gives her a warning about compliments from friendly people. People say it is a great idea because it costs them nothing, so Mira must watch what they do, not what they say.
Mira practises her interview on Kofi in the workshop. He answers very politely, and she realises that a nice answer is not the same as a useful one.
Kofi also teaches her how to follow up on each answer. She adds questions like what happened next, what did you do instead, and who helped you?
Mira realises that she does this every day at the hospital. She asks patients what happened and listens carefully, and she knows not to put words in their mouths.
Mira writes her five questions on a small card. She plans to knock on ten doors along Alder Street, and she will ask each neighbour to tell a story.
The first door belongs to Anya, who invites Mira in for tea. Anya says that she last needed a ladder in spring, so she drove across town to borrow her brother's.
Anya adds that she once bought a cheap tool for one job. It broke on the very first day, and she had to buy a second one anyway.
Tomas says he lends tools freely to his nephews and old friends. Once he lent a pipe wrench to someone he barely knew, and he never saw it again.
Priya has just moved to Alder Street with almost nothing. She asked her landlord for a drill, he said no, and her shelves have been leaning against the wall for weeks.
Mrs Haddad, who runs the café at the corner, says she once needed a big floor sander for one day. She hired one, but it was costly and heavy, and she nearly hurt her back.
A young father at number twenty tells her that he is always short of time. When he needs something, he usually buys the cheapest version and complains about it later.
Mira writes down people's exact words and leaves her own ideas out. Twice she feels the urge to describe Toolshelf, and twice she stops herself and asks another question.
One neighbour says he has no time and closes the door before she can ask. Mira feels embarrassed, but she writes down what happened and notes that busy people may not borrow at all.
Mr Reyes, who owns the hardware shop on Alder Street, is her ninth visit. He tells her that customers ask him every week whether he has a tool they could simply borrow.
After the tenth visit, Mira sits on a wall at sunset with a notebook full of stories. She is tired, but she feels she has learned more in a week than in a month of planning.
Mira spreads her pages across the floor and goes through them with two coloured pens. She underlines what people did in blue, and what they said they might do in green.
A clear pattern appears in her notes almost at once. Almost everyone has borrowed tools from family and friends, and they did it easily, without a second thought.
The second pattern is just as clear to her. Strangers almost never lend, and only Tomas had ever tried it, so he lost his wrench.
Mira looks again at her riskiest guess, and it does not look good. Even generous people lend only to those they know, and Toolshelf was built for neighbours who hardly meet.
She counts the answers very carefully, one page after another. Of the nine neighbours who spoke to her, seven had borrowed a tool from someone they knew, and not one had borrowed from a stranger.
Then she sees another pattern hidden in the same notes. The real problem is not that people lack tools, but that they cannot quickly find the right one or trust the person who owns it.
She sees that all the stories fit together well. Anya drove across town, Priya hung no shelves, and Mrs Haddad hired a machine, because nobody knew who nearby had what they needed.
Mira tells Kofi she is disappointed, because her app does not solve the problem she imagined. Kofi grins and says that she found this out in one week instead of one year.
Mira reshapes her idea once more, using what she has learned. Toolshelf should not be a market for strangers, but a way to know who owns what and who can be trusted with it.
She puts a new note at the top of the wall. Her new riskiest guess is that neighbours will lend tools once they know who is asking and who is borrowing.
Kofi explains that the smallest test is not a smaller app. It is a tiny experiment aimed straight at the riskiest guess, and nothing else.
Lucas calls again that week, and this time he has a very tempting offer. He can build a simple app in a month, but Mira sees that it would still be a lot of work for one question.
Mira asks herself a completely new question about the whole test. What is the cheapest, quickest thing she could do that would show whether neighbours will lend tools when they know who is asking?
At last she has found the answer she needs. She will make a paper list of tools that neighbours will lend, pin it up on one street, and add her phone number.
Here is exactly how the small test will work in practice. Neighbours tell Mira which tools they could lend, she writes them on the list, and she arranges the handover herself whenever someone calls.
Mira will run the whole service entirely by hand. It would never work for a thousand people, but it will teach her exactly what each person needs.
There is another advantage to doing it by hand. Mira will see every request herself, and she will hear every worry and every small surprise.
Mira sets very clear limits for her test, and she writes them down. It will cover only Alder Street, it will last two weeks, and each loan will be for a few days at most.
Dina reads the plan and says that it seems too small to prove anything. Mira smiles and says that it is small on purpose, because the goal is to learn, not to impress anyone.
Mira puts the whole plan on a single page with three headings: the guess, the test, and what she will count. She notices that the last heading is still blank.
Kofi tells her that she must decide what success looks like before the test starts. Afterwards, he warns, everyone finds a reason to call the result a win.
Kofi tells her a story from his own life. He once made ten chairs and sold three, and because he had set no target, he told himself that this was a good result.
Mira asks Dina to help her choose a number. It should not be so easy that she cannot fail, and not so hard that nothing could ever pass.
Dina points out that the target should count a real action. A promise or a sign-up is only words, but a tool that really leaves a garage is a fact.
Together they decide on a clear target that they both feel is fair. If at least five of the twenty households lend a tool within two weeks, Mira will count the test as a success.
Mira signs the page with the target and the date. Then she gives a copy to Kofi, so that nobody can change the rules when the results arrive.
Mira goes one step further than she did before, and plans ahead. She writes down what she will do if the result is good, what she will do if it is poor, and when she would stop.
Mira chooses twenty houses along Alder Street and marks them on a map. She picks a mixture: old and new neighbours, big gardens and small flats.
Mira writes a short and friendly leaflet in very plain words. It asks neighbours whether they have a tool they could lend, and it gives her phone number and the dates of the test.
