It costs almost nothing, it requires no software, and it can begin the following morning, long before a single screen has been designed. The simplicity of it was almost insulting, and Mira wondered why she had not thought of it herself.

Mira asked, rather eagerly, whether she should simply describe Toolshelf to each neighbour and ask whether they liked it. Kofi winced as though she had dropped a heavy chisel on his foot, and he shook his head slowly. That, he said, was almost the worst thing she could do, because it invited people to be kind rather than honest.

Questions about the future, Kofi explained, almost always produce cheerful answers, as in whether someone would lend a tool next month. People sincerely mean what they say in the moment, and they imagine a better, more generous version of themselves, but the real person who turns up next month is often busier and warier. A promise about tomorrow, he said, is the cheapest thing a neighbour can give you.

Good questions, Kofi went on, ask about what people actually did, not about what they imagine they might do. The past is solid, and it holds real choices, real irritations and real workarounds, whereas the future is only a hopeful story. If you want to know what a person will do, he said, find out what they did the last time the same thing happened.

Mira began to draft her first question, which asked each neighbour to tell her about the last time they had needed a tool they did not own. What had they actually done about it, she wanted to know, and how had the whole thing turned out for them? It was a modest, almost dull question, and she suspected it might be worth more than any slogan she had ever written.

Kofi then warned her about compliments, which are the most pleasant and least useful answers a person can receive. A neighbour who says that Toolshelf is a wonderful idea has risked nothing and promised nothing, so the remark teaches you nothing at all. What counts, he said, is behaviour: who made time, who went out of their way, and who actually did something.

They rehearsed in the workshop, with Mira asking her questions and Kofi playing a neighbour. He turned out to be too gracious an actor, answering every question with such courtesy that she learned almost nothing from him. She saw that a friendly reply can be a closed door, and that she would have to ask what happened next.

Kofi taught her the value of the follow-up, which is the small question that opens a door the first question only knocked on. She added what happened next, what did you do instead, and who helped you, all in the plainest words she could find. Each was short and each invited a story, and stories, she was beginning to understand, are made of facts.

Mira suddenly realised that she had been doing this for years, in a different uniform. At the hospital she asked patients what had happened, listened without hurrying, and wrote down what they said rather than what she expected them to say. The skill she needed was one she already possessed, and the thought gave her a quiet surge of confidence.

By evening Mira had a small card with five short questions on it, each aimed at a real event rather than an opinion. She planned to knock on ten doors along Alder Street, to ask for ten minutes at each, and to listen to ten stories without selling anything. It was the least glamorous project she had ever started, and she was a little afraid of it.

The first door belonged to Anya, a warm and talkative neighbour who put the kettle on before Mira had finished her introduction. When asked about the last time she needed a tool she did not own, Anya described borrowing a ladder to clean her gutters. She had driven across town to fetch it from her brother, who had also given her a long lecture about safety.

Anya, once she had properly begun, found that there was a good deal more to tell her. She had once bought a cheap tool for a single repair, and it had snapped in her hand before the job was half done, so that she had to buy a better one anyway. She laughed at the memory, but Mira noticed that she remembered the exact price and was still a little annoyed about it.

Tomas received her with grave courtesy and said that he lent his tools freely to his nephews and to the friends he had known for decades. Once, long ago, he had made the mistake of lending a good pipe wrench to a man he barely knew, and the wrench had never come home. He told the story with the calm of a man who has accepted a loss but has certainly not forgotten it.

Priya had moved into a small flat on Alder Street only a month earlier, with two suitcases and almost no belongings. She had bought shelves but had no drill to hang them, and when she asked her landlord, he told her briskly that it was not his problem. The shelves were still leaning against the wall, and she explained, somewhat sheepishly, that she did not know a single neighbour well enough to ask.

Mrs Haddad, who ran the café on the corner, remembered the week she had needed to sand the floor of the dining room before a reopening. She had hired a machine for a single day, paid far more than she expected, and nearly strained her back carrying it up the steps. She had never thought to ask a neighbour, she admitted, because it had not occurred to her that a neighbour might own one.

At number twenty, a young father with a baby on his shoulder told Mira that he never had time to ask anybody for anything. Whenever a job came up, he bought the cheapest tool he could find, grumbled about the price, and promptly forgot where he had put it. His garage, he said with a rueful smile, was a graveyard of one-use purchases.

Mira filled page after page with exact quotations, resisting the temptation to translate what people said into what she wanted to hear. Twice she felt the old enthusiasm rising and an urge to describe Toolshelf, and both times she bit her tongue and asked another question instead. It was a great deal harder than she had expected it to be, and also far more revealing.

At the seventh house, a man in a hurry said that he had no time for questions and closed the door on her mid-sentence. Mira stood on the step for a moment, her cheeks warm, and then wrote it down in her notebook as faithfully as all the rest. A refusal, she reminded herself, is also data, and it suggested that some people would never give a stranger a minute, let alone a drill.

The ninth visit was to Mr Reyes, the owner of the hardware shop on Alder Street, who leaned on his counter and thought carefully before he answered. Every week, he said, someone came in asking whether they could borrow a tool for a single job, and every week he told them no, because tools that leave a shop rarely come back. He added that he sometimes felt sorry for the customers, who left looking quite disappointed.

When the tenth conversation was over, Mira sat on a low garden wall as the sun went down, with a notebook swollen with other people's stories. She was tired, her feet ached, and she had been refused once, but she felt she had learned more in a single week than in all her weeks of planning. The only thing left to do was to read the notes with an open mind.

Mira spread her ten stories across the floor of her living room and read through them with two coloured pens. She underlined what people had actually done in blue and what they had merely said they might do in green, and she was struck by how much blue there was. The past, once she looked at it properly, was far more informative than any amount of enthusiasm.

The first pattern was impossible to miss: nearly everyone she had spoken to had borrowed tools, and almost all of it had happened within a small circle of family and friends. It was done casually and warmly, with no forms and no fuss, and sometimes the tool stayed away for months without anyone minding. Borrowing, it seemed, was alive and well, but only among people who already trusted each other.

The second pattern was equally clear to her, and it was a great deal less welcome than the first. Hardly anyone had ever lent a tool to a stranger, and the only person who had tried, Tomas, still spoke of his lost wrench with the weary dignity of a man who has been wronged. Trust, it seemed, was the currency of lending, and neighbours who barely knew each other had very little of it.

Mira looked again at the note at the top of her wall, and her stomach sank. Generous people, it seemed, were generous only to those they already knew, and Toolshelf had been designed for neighbours who hardly spoke. Her riskiest guess had not been confirmed, and in its original form it was looking very unlikely to survive.

She counted carefully, because impressions can deceive and numbers, even small ones, concentrate the mind. Of the nine neighbours who had talked to her, seven had borrowed a tool from someone they knew within the past year, and not one had ever borrowed from a stranger. Nine people proved nothing in a scientific sense, but they were more than Mira had had a week earlier.

Then a deeper pattern emerged from the pages, one that she had not been looking for at all. The problem was not that people lacked tools, since the street was full of them, but that nobody could quickly find the right one or feel safe asking its owner. The shortage, in other words, was one of information and trust rather than of drills.

She drew green lines between the stories and saw that they were one story told three ways. Anya had driven across town for a ladder that a neighbour might have lent her, Priya had left her shelves leaning against a wall, and Mrs Haddad had hired a machine that probably sat in a garage nearby. In every case the tool existed nearby, but the person who needed it had no way to know.

Mira confessed to Kofi that she felt deflated, because the answer she had found was not the one she had hoped for. He grinned broadly and told her that this was precisely what she wanted, since she had learned in one week what could have cost her a year. A disappointing fact, he said, is worth far more than a flattering fantasy, and the sooner it arrives, the cheaper it is.

Mira took a clean page and began again, this time with the problem in the middle. Toolshelf would not be a market in which strangers traded drills, but a simple way for neighbours to know who owned what and who could be trusted to look after it. The idea was humbler than the one she had started with, but for the first time it rested on something she had actually seen.

Mira stuck a fresh note above all the others, and it carried a more careful guess than before. Neighbours, she now believed, would lend their tools if they knew who would be borrowing and could trust the arrangement. Before she believed it too firmly, however, she resolved to find a way of testing it that would cost almost nothing at all.

Kofi explained that a small test is not a small version of the whole product, which is a mistake that many people make. It is a tiny experiment aimed squarely at the riskiest guess, and anything in it that does not serve that purpose should be cut away. The real trick, he said, is to resist building the pleasant and impressive parts of the idea first.

Lucas telephoned again with an attractive proposal: he could build a stripped-down version of the app in about a month, in his evenings, and for no charge. Mira was tempted, because it sounded so modest, but she saw that a month of coding is still a very large effort to spend on a single question. A smaller app, she realised, is still an app, and her question did not need one.

Mira began to ask herself a different kind of question: what was the cheapest and quickest thing she could do that would show whether neighbours would lend their tools to each other? She listed a few ideas, from a poster in a window to a telephone call tree, and crossed them out as she went. The better ones were all surprisingly dull, which she took as a good sign.

At last she found something suitably humble: a paper list of tools that neighbours were willing to lend, pinned up on one street with her own telephone number at the bottom. Anyone wanting a tool would call her, and she would arrange the loan herself. There was no software and no map, and the entire cost was a few sheets of paper and some tape.

The mechanics of the new test were really quite wonderfully simple, and she could explain them in one breath. Neighbours would tell Mira which tools they were willing to lend, she would add them to the list, and whenever someone telephoned, she would arrange the handover and, if necessary, stand beside it. It was a service made of paper and good manners, and it contained everything the test needed.

Mira resolved to run the whole service by hand, answering the calls and arranging the loans herself, even though such a system could never serve a thousand people. That was exactly the point, because the purpose of the test was to learn rather than to scale. A service that does not scale can still teach you what is worth scaling.

There was a further advantage to working by hand, which was that nothing would pass through a screen on its way to her. She would hear every request, every hesitation and every worry in people's own words, and she would see in person what a machine would have hidden. Software, she thought, was a way of hiding those details, and she needed them for now.

She was careful to keep the test small and tightly bounded, as a good experiment should be. It would cover only Alder Street, run for exactly two weeks, and involve only loans of a few days each, so that nothing could grow beyond her ability to follow it. A small boundary, she was learning, makes it easier to see what is really happening inside it.

Dina read the one-page plan and observed, with the frankness of a sister, that it seemed very small and not at all impressive. Mira laughed and agreed, saying that the test was small on purpose, because its aim was to teach her something and not to look grand. A small test that gives a clear answer, she said, is worth more than a grand one that gives none.

Mira wrote the whole plan on a single page under three headings: the guess she was testing, the test she would run and the thing she would count at the end. The first two sections filled quickly, but she noticed that the third was still blank. It was, she realised, the most important heading on the page, and she was not yet sure what to put under it.

Kofi insisted that Mira must decide what success would look like before the test began, and not a moment later. Once the results are in, he warned, the human mind becomes remarkably inventive, and almost any outcome can be described as encouraging. Fixing the target beforehand, he said, is the only dependable way to keep yourself completely honest.

Kofi then told her a rather embarrassing story against himself, to make his point clearly. Years ago he had made ten chairs for a market stall and sold three, and because he had never decided what a good result would be, he had declared himself pleased. Only later, doing the sums, had he understood that three sales did not even cover the wood.

Mira asked Dina to help her choose the number, and the two of them spent an evening arguing happily over it. A target so modest that she could not fail would teach her nothing, but one so ambitious that nobody could reach it would be equally useless. The right number, they agreed, was one that would feel like a genuine signal if she hit it and a genuine warning if she did not.

Dina pointed out that the target should be measured in real actions and not in promises, interest or compliments. A tool that actually left a garage and arrived in another pair of hands was a fact, whereas a sign-up was only a polite thought. If the test measured the wrong thing, she said, it would only be an expensive way of being cheered up.

In the end they settled on a figure that felt both fair and a little frightening. If at least five of the twenty households on the list actually lent a tool within two weeks, Mira would call the test a success, and if fewer than five did, she would not. She wrote it in large letters and underlined it twice, so that she could not argue with it later.

To make it binding, Mira signed the page, dated it, and handed a copy to Kofi, who put it in a drawer of his workbench with some solemnity. It was a slightly theatrical gesture, but it served a serious purpose, because it made the target hard to quietly forget. Anyone can quietly move a goalpost that exists only in their own head, but nobody can move one that is written down.

Mira took the idea a step further and decided in advance what she would do with each possible result. A strong result would let her carry on, a weak one would force her to think again, and a very poor one would be a sign to stop. Having the decisions ready before the numbers arrived meant that she would not be swayed by her mood on the day.

Mira picked twenty houses along Alder Street and marked each on a hand-drawn map, taking care to include a mixture of old residents and newcomers, big gardens and small flats. She deliberately did not choose only her friends, because friends would flatter the result. A fair test, she reminded herself, has to meet people who owe her nothing.

She wrote a short leaflet in plain, friendly words, asking neighbours whether they owned a tool they might lend for a few days and giving her telephone number and the dates of the test. She resisted the urge to make it clever or to mention any app, because the message was simply an invitation to help one another. Then she printed twenty copies on her old home printer and watched each one slide warm into the tray.

On a bright Saturday morning Mira walked the length of Alder Street, pushing a leaflet through twenty letterboxes with a hammering heart. When the last one had dropped onto a doormat, she went home, sat at the kitchen table and placed her telephone in front of her. The experiment had begun, and for the first time in months there was nothing left for her to plan.

The first day of the experiment passed in an unbroken and rather heavy silence. Mira checked her telephone every ten minutes, made three cups of tea she did not want, and told herself repeatedly that people take time to read their post. By evening, however, the quiet had begun to feel like a verdict, and she had to remind herself that it was far too early to judge.

On the second morning the telephone finally rang, and Mira snatched it up before the second ring. It was Anya, who declared warmly that Toolshelf was a wonderful idea and that the street really needed something like it. She did not mention any tool she might lend, and Mira, writing the call down, was careful to put it in the column marked words.

Over the next few days a small but steady stream of encouragement flowed in from the street. Notes appeared under her door, a neighbour called across the road to tell her what a lovely thought it was, and a stranger at the bus stop squeezed her arm and wished her luck. Each kindness was genuine, and each made her heart lift a little before her good sense caught up.

Mira felt a warm glow of satisfaction, and she was quite aware of a quiet temptation to count all this goodwill as success. A voice in her head reasoned that so many people could not be wrong, and that the experiment must be going splendidly. It was the voice of hope rather than of evidence, and she had been warned about it.

Mira drew a line down the middle of a page and kept two columns, with kind words on the left and real actions on the right. The left column filled quickly and the right column stayed stubbornly empty, which taught her something before the test had even finished. She had agreed that only a tool leaving a garage would count, and she held herself to it.

On the fifth day Tomas telephoned her at home, speaking slowly and with his usual old-fashioned formality. He had been thinking it over, he said, and he would like to put his router and his tile cutter on the list, provided that Mira herself took charge of them. It was the first real action, and Mira wrote it in the right-hand column with a hand that trembled slightly.

That same afternoon Priya telephoned, and Mira arranged for a neighbour's drill to travel the short distance to her flat. By evening the long-leaning shelves were fixed to the wall and loaded with books, and Priya sent a delighted message full of exclamation marks. It was a tiny triumph, but it proved that the idea could work for at least one person.

In the second week the telephone grew quieter and the initial excitement seemed to evaporate. When Mira gently followed up with those who had sounded most enthusiastic, they said they would think about it, or that they had been very busy, or that they would certainly be in touch. She had heard enough courteous evasions at the hospital over the years to recognise them quickly.

At the end of the fortnight Mira sat down with her two columns and counted them with great care. Fourteen people had said that they would love to take part, but only three had actually offered a tool, and one of those was Tomas, who had been willing to lend before anyone knocked on his door. The gap between those two numbers was enormous, and she looked at it for quite some time.

She laid the result beside the target she had signed two weeks earlier, and the comparison was brutally simple. Three lenders fell short of five, and since the rule had been written before the experiment began, there was nothing to explain away or soften. It stung, and yet there was a peculiar relief in a result that was too clear to argue with.

Mira wrote the lesson of the fortnight at the top of a clean page, in a single plain sentence. Many people say yes, she noted, but far fewer actually do anything, and the distance between those two groups is very much larger than it feels in the glow of a friendly conversation. She underlined the word actually twice, so that she could never forget how much it mattered.

Mira saw that fourteen people wanting to join sounded impressive, and that she could have announced a triumph to her friends and believed it herself. Large, flattering numbers like sign-ups, likes and interested replies are comfortable precisely because they cost the people behind them nothing. They can sit on a page looking splendid while the thing that matters stays empty.

Dina, sitting in her small bakery office, listened to the whole story and nodded slowly. A figure that only ever rises, she said, is one that has been chosen because it cannot disappoint you, and it deserves the deepest suspicion. The numbers worth watching are those that could easily go down, such as how many people actually do something and how many come back.

Mira realised that the most valuable people to talk to were no longer the enthusiasts but the eleven who had said yes and then done nothing. They knew something she did not, which was what had held them back, and she was determined to find out without making anyone feel accused. She wrote a short, friendly script that asked what had happened and promised that there were no wrong answers.

The first man she telephoned was honest at once and rather apologetic about it. His power tools were expensive and carefully kept, he explained, and the thought of a stranger dropping or misusing one made him feel physically uneasy. He had meant what he said about liking the idea, but the picture of his saw in an unknown garage was more than he could face.

A woman living further along the street told her a short and rather rueful story. She had lent a ladder to someone only once, and it had never come back, and although the loss was small, the feeling of having been taken for granted lasted far longer than the ladder would have. She said that she liked Mira's idea very much, but that her trust had already been spent.

Others gave a more practical reason, which was that the arrangement itself felt like work. Between jobs, children and tired evenings, the thought of agreeing a time to hand over a tool and then arranging another to collect it seemed like one more small chore in an already crowded week. The generosity was certainly there in these people, but it was not enough to overcome the effort.

Anya was the most candid of them all, and she laughed at herself as she explained. She had said yes simply because Mira had been so pleasant on the doorstep, and it had felt rude to say anything else, so she had agreed without giving the idea a moment's real thought. Mira thanked her sincerely, because that confession was worth more than a dozen compliments.

When all of the calls were over, Mira sorted the reasons into four separate piles on the table. People feared that their tools would be damaged, they feared that the tools would never return, they found the handover an irritation, and above all they did not know the borrower. Almost nobody had said that the idea was bad, and every reason was about risk and not about need.

Then a small but important detail struck her about the three people who had lent. Each of them knew her personally, and each had been reassured by the fact that she, a familiar face, would be standing between them and the borrower. Trust, she realised, had not come from the paper or the idea but from the person in the middle.

Kofi pointed out that every honest experiment ends in a decision with three possible forms. You may carry on exactly as before if the evidence is strong, change direction if it is mixed, or stop altogether if the idea has clearly failed. What matters is that the choice is made deliberately, in the light of evidence, and not by default or by habit.

Mira considered the first option carefully for some time, and then she rejected it rather quickly. The evidence was weak, and repeating the same experiment with more leaflets and a friendlier smile would have been stubbornness dressed up as determination. A method that has just failed should not be repeated simply because the person using it feels committed.

Stopping, she decided, would be just as hasty, because the test had also revealed something encouraging. The need was real, as Priya's empty wall, Anya's long drive and Mrs Haddad's hired machine all demonstrated, and what had failed was not the problem but the particular way she had tried to solve it. A weak method, she told herself, is not the same thing as a worthless idea.

That left the middle path, which was to change course in some meaningful way. The question that mattered was what small adjustment could answer the fears she had heard, and she kept returning to one phrase from her notes, which was the need for someone people already trusted. She looked down Alder Street and tried to think who that person might be.

Then the answer arrived, so obvious that she wondered how she had missed it. Mr Reyes had kept his hardware shop on Alder Street for most of his working life, everyone knew him, and every week somebody asked him whether he could lend them a tool. He was already, without having planned it, the most trusted tool person for several streets around.

Mira changed the whole plan in one short sentence that she wrote on a fresh page. Instead of neighbours lending directly to neighbours, donated and shared tools would sit on a shelf in a trusted shop, from which anyone could borrow them for a few days. The idea of Toolshelf survived, but its shape had changed completely, and it had changed because of what real people had told her.

She checked the new plan against each of the four fears in turn and was pleased with the results. A shop could inspect tools when they came back, keep a simple record of who had what, offer a single convenient place for handovers, and know its customers by sight. No plan could remove every worry, but this one at least answered the ones she had been told about.

Kofi asked, with an expression of exaggerated innocence, whether the failed test had been a waste. Mira added up the cost with some care: two weeks of evenings, twenty sheets of paper, a roll of tape and a good many minutes on the telephone. It was a remarkably small bill for everything that she had gained from the whole experience.

Mira set that small cost beside the twelve months and the savings she had once been prepared to spend, and the contrast made her laugh aloud. She would have discovered exactly the same lessons, but late, expensively and at a moment when changing course would have been almost impossible. A test that fails cheaply, Kofi said with satisfaction, has done precisely what a test is for.

Mira took the signed target page back out of Kofi's drawer and wrote across the bottom of it, in her tidiest hand, the words missed, but learned. She felt lighter than she had in weeks, because failure no longer looked like a verdict but like a piece of information. Tomorrow morning, she decided, she would go and talk to Mr Reyes about the idea of a shelf.

Early the next morning, before the shutters had gone up, Mira knocked on the door of Mr Reyes's shop and asked for ten minutes of his time. She told him honestly what her first test had shown, including its failure, and she explained the change she had in mind. She was careful not to oversell, because she had learned that enthusiasm is a poor substitute for evidence.

Mr Reyes listened without interrupting, and then he set out his worries with the clarity of a man who has run a shop for decades. If people could borrow tools, he asked, why would they ever buy them from him, and what would he do when the tools disappeared? They were fair questions, and Mira was glad that he had put them so directly.

Mira did not argue, because she knew that a promise could not answer a worry, and instead she proposed a small trial of one month. The tools would be donated by her and her neighbours, they would sit on a single shelf in a corner of the shop, and she would personally cover any that went missing. Moreover, she added, the experiment would show him in plain figures whether borrowers also became buyers of other things.

Mr Reyes stroked his chin for a long moment while the clock on the wall ticked loudly in the quiet shop. Then he said that he was curious, that a month on a single shelf was a small price to pay for finding out, and that he would give it a try. They shook hands, and Mira felt as though she had been granted something much larger than a corner of a shop.

Before a single tool was moved, Mira wrote down the new guess that the second test would examine. People would borrow tools from a shelf in a trusted shop, she wrote, and they would bring them back in good condition and on time. She had learned to put her hopes into a form that reality could contradict.

Again, before the test began, Mira and Dina sat down to write the target, and this time they were more careful about what counted. They agreed on at least ten loans in the month, nearly every tool returned, and at least four people who came back to borrow a second time. She signed the page and gave a copy to Kofi, who smiled and placed it beside the first.

Word travelled, and over the next few days neighbours began to turn up at the shop with tools under their arms. Tomas brought his router and tile cutter, Kofi contributed a set of clamps and a spirit level, and Mrs Haddad carried in a small stepladder. By Friday there were twelve tools in all, which was a far better harvest than her leaflets had produced.

Kofi built a plain pine shelf in a single afternoon and screwed it firmly to the wall, saying that it was the easiest job he had been asked to do in years. Mira gave each tool a simple label with its name, a number and a short note explaining how to handle it with care. The shelf looked modest, but it had an air of quiet order that she found strangely moving.

Once again she kept the machinery as simple as possible, deliberately avoiding any software. A small paper book hung beside the shelf on a string, and each loan was recorded in it with the borrower's name, the tool, the date and a promise to return it. Everything was done by hand, so Mira could see precisely what was happening, and nothing was hidden from her.

On the opening day Mira stood near the new shelf at lunchtime with a cup of tea she did not drink, trying to look relaxed and failing. She watched the door every time it opened, and every time the customer walked straight past the shelf to the nails or the paint. Mr Reyes, in the middle of all this, was calmly weighing a bag of screws and pretending that nothing unusual was happening.

At three o'clock the door opened and in walked Ben, Anya's teenage son, looking slightly embarrassed to be asking. He needed a spirit level for a woodwork project at school, he explained, and had no wish to buy one he would use once. He wrote his name in the paper book with great care, and Mira felt a wave of relief that she tried very hard not to show.

By the time Mr Reyes turned the sign on the door, two tools had been borrowed, a spirit level and a set of clamps. It was a modest beginning, but it was two more real actions than she had seen on the first day of her paper experiment. She wrote both loans neatly into her tally and went home feeling cautiously, quietly encouraged.

By the end of the first week, seven tools had gone out, and Mira studied the names in the paper book with growing interest. Some of the borrowers were people she had never imagined as customers, while several of those who had cheered her loudest in the first test had not appeared at all. The shelf, it seemed, was telling her something about the street that her plans had not.

Mira stopped trying to please everyone and began to look for the people who needed the shelf most. Three groups stood out clearly from the names in the book: new tenants setting up a home, new parents with endless small jobs to do, and weekend hobbyists who wanted a special tool for a day. These were the people for whom owning a tool made the least sense and borrowing the most.

A new father came in one evening to borrow a drill so that he could fix a safety gate at the top of his stairs. He told Mira that he would never have dreamed of knocking on a neighbour's door, but taking something from a shop shelf felt entirely natural. That small remark confirmed everything that her interviews had suggested to her about trust.

A weekend hobbyist, who confessed to a dream of building furniture one day, borrowed a jigsaw to make a bird box for his garden. He returned it two days later, wiped clean and with a sheet of sandpaper tucked in as a thank-you. He showed Mira a photograph of the finished box on his phone with obvious pride.

Mira began to pay particular attention to the names that appeared more than once in the paper book. A person who borrows a tool once may merely have been curious or polite, but a person who returns for a second time has found genuine value, and no compliment could ever say so as loudly. Repeat visits, she wrote in her notebook, are the most honest thing a customer can offer.

In the second week Priya walked back into the shop to borrow a paint roller and a stepladder, since she had decided to redecorate her flat. She had brought a friend who had just moved to the next street, and she announced to the shop in general that this was where you came when you had nothing. Mira, standing quietly in the corner of the shop, could scarcely contain her delight at all.

At closing time Mr Reyes mentioned, in his dry way, that a surprising number of the borrowers had also bought something while they were in the shop. Screws, sandpaper, paint and drill bits were all leaving his shelves a little faster than usual, since people who borrow a tool still need things to use it with. His earlier worry about lost sales, he admitted with a shrug, was looking a good deal smaller now.

At the end of the second week Mira sat in the quiet shop and counted fourteen loans and four borrowers who had returned a second time. Both figures already reached the target she had signed, with two weeks still to go, and she allowed herself a small, careful smile. She did not announce a victory, because she knew that early results can flatter, and she wanted to see the whole month.

When the month ended, Mira sat with Mr Reyes and totalled the results in the paper book. There had been twenty-six loans, every tool but one had returned, and six people had come back for a second time, which beat the target she had signed. Mr Reyes, to her great delight, asked whether the shelf might please stay in his shop for good.

Success, as it often does, set Mira's imagination racing, and she found herself sketching five shops, a delivery van and an elegant website. For one evening the old fever returned, and the twelve-month plan in her drawer began to seem like a modest first step. She had to remind herself that one good month on one shelf was exactly that and no more.

Kofi laughed out loud at the five-shop sketch, though not unkindly, and then told her what he believed. Small steps beat big launches, he said, because a person who tries a little and adjusts can correct mistakes while they are still cheap, whereas a person who delivers everything at once discovers them in public. Ambition was perfectly fine, he said, but it should arrive in small instalments and not in one great lump.

Kofi gave an example from his own trade, which was that he never built a complete cupboard before checking the very first joint. A flaw at the start, he said, spreads quietly through everything built on top of it, and by the time you see it, you have no choice but to start again. A new venture is no different, he added, except that the wood is made of time and savings.

Mira devised a rhythm that she could follow without fuss: each week she would choose one guess, run a small test of it, count what actually happened, and decide what to do next. She wrote the four steps in large letters on a sheet of paper and pinned it above her kitchen table. It was nothing more than a habit, but it turned out to be the most valuable tool she owned.

For her very first weekly cycle, Mira chose a modest and cheap guess about the tool labels. She suspected that people would borrow more readily if each tool was marked with the job it did, such as hang a shelf or cut a tile, rather than just the name of the tool. Most people, she reasoned, do not wake up wanting a router, but they do wake up wanting a shelf.

After a single week with the new labels, Mira counted the loans of the relabelled tools and found that they had risen from three to five. It was a small difference, and she was careful not to treat it as proof, but it pointed the right way and had cost her only a few strips of tape. She decided to keep the labels and to test something else the following Sunday.

After six weeks, Mira had six weekly sheets pinned in a neat row along her kitchen wall, each recording a guess, a test and a result. She noticed that she had built almost nothing in that time, yet she had learned more than in the whole of the previous year. The speed that counted, she understood, was the speed of learning, and every cycle she completed made her a little wiser.

Mira set herself a small monthly budget for Toolshelf and left the rest of her savings untouched, a decision that Dina approved with unusual warmth. She found, rather to her surprise, that spending slowly made her think far more clearly, because every purchase had to justify itself. Plenty of money, she suspected, is just a way of postponing the moment when you must be honest.

With a limited budget in front of her, Mira acquired the habit of asking a new question before every expense. Was there a cheaper way to learn the same thing, she wondered, and was the answer really worth the price she would pay? More often than not, there was a cheaper way, and more often than not it taught her just as much.

Everything on the shelf so far had been free, and Mira knew very well that people will accept almost anything that costs them nothing. A polite yes is easy to give, whereas a payment is a small act of commitment, and she needed to know whether the shelf was valued enough to deserve one. Without income, she realised, Toolshelf would remain a pleasant hobby and never become a lasting service.

Mira pinned a new note to her wall, and it held a guess that mattered a great deal. People, she wrote, would pay a small fee to borrow a tool from the shelf, even though they had seen it offered for nothing. If the guess were wrong, the shelf could not support itself, and no amount of goodwill would keep it alive for long.

Mira recalled everything she had learned about questions concerning the future, and she saw immediately that asking people whether they would pay was a trap. Everyone would say yes, kindly and quite sincerely, and the answer would be completely worthless to her. The only reliable test was to charge a small fee for a week and watch what real borrowers did.

Kofi advised her on the amount of the fee, and his advice was characteristically down to earth. The fee should be low enough that no neighbour felt cheated, but not so low that it became a joke, since a price that nobody notices tells you nothing about value. They settled on roughly the cost of a cup of coffee in the café on the corner.

As always, she wrote the target before the test, and she was strict with herself about it. If at least six of the next ten borrowers still chose to borrow after being told about the fee, she would treat the guess as supported, and if not, she would think again. Dina signed as witness this time, with a flourish that made them both laugh.

Mira did not want to spring the fee on anyone, so she wrote a small and honest sign for the shelf. It explained that a modest fee would help to keep the tools in good repair and replace those that wore out, and it thanked people for supporting the shelf. She believed that a person who understands what a price is for will pay it far more willingly.

The reactions were as varied as the borrowers themselves, and she found them fascinating to watch. One man grumbled a little and then paid anyway, a woman asked politely whether the money really went to the tools, and a young tenant handed over his coin with a grin. Mira listened to all of it, wrote everything down in her notebook, and noticed that the young tenant added that it was still far cheaper than buying a drill.

At the end of the week Mira counted the results, and the answer was clear. Out of ten borrowers who had been told about the fee, eight still went ahead and borrowed, which comfortably beat her target of six. The guess that people would pay had been tested with real coins and real borrowers, and it had passed.

Mira also telephoned the two borrowers who had chosen not to go ahead, and what they said was interesting. One had needed a tool for only five minutes, and the fee seemed out of proportion to a job that small, while the other had simply forgotten to bring any money. Both reasons suggested adjustments rather than a failure, and she wrote down several possible fixes.

Mira reflected on the result for a while, with a mixture of satisfaction and caution. Eight real payments were worth more than any quantity of compliments, but ten borrowers was still a very small number, and she knew that a small group can mislead as easily as it can inform. She resolved to repeat the test with new borrowers over the coming weeks before she trusted it completely.

Over coffee at the bakery, Dina asked a question that Mira had never considered, which was what it cost her to find each new borrower. When she added up the leaflets, the tape, the signs and the hours she had spent, the total was larger than she had expected. It had never occurred to her that bringing in a customer was itself something that could be priced.

Mira divided what she had spent by the number of new borrowers it had brought, and the result was what is called the cost of finding a customer. It was an unglamorous figure, but it was among the most useful she had ever calculated, because it showed what each new person truly cost. Until then she had been spending money without any idea of what it bought.

Next she estimated what a typical borrower might pay over the course of a year, by looking at how often the regulars came and what the fee had been. If a customer visited four times a year and paid a small fee on each occasion, the sum was easy to calculate. Then came the interesting part, which was to place the two numbers side by side.

Dina explained the rule in a single breath, with the air of someone who had seen the mistake made many times. If it costs more to find a customer than that customer will ever pay, then every new customer makes the venture poorer, and growth becomes a faster way of losing money. The numbers had to work for a single borrower before they could work for a thousand.

As an experiment, Mira paid for a second, glossier round of leaflets and counted carefully what it produced. Only three new borrowers appeared, and when she divided the cost by three, the cost of finding each was higher than any of them were likely to pay in a year. It was a clear and rather humbling result, and she crossed leaflets off her list.

Watching the door in the quiet hours, Mira began to notice that many of the new faces arrived in the company of someone she already knew. Priya had brought a friend, and a pair of neighbours who had both borrowed in the same week appeared to have heard about it from the same chat over a fence. She suspected that the shelf was spreading by itself, but a suspicion was not enough.

To be sure, Mira added one more line to the paper book, which asked each new borrower how they had heard about the shelf. It was the cheapest research she could have invented, since it needed no software and no survey, and it took each person only a few seconds. She promised herself that she would keep the answers for a month before drawing any conclusion.

At the end of the month Mira read the answers through, and the pattern was unmistakable. Of thirty new borrowers, nineteen had heard about the shelf from a friend or a neighbour, six had noticed it in the shop window, three had received a leaflet, and two gave other answers. Most people, in other words, had come because somebody they knew had told them.

Mrs Haddad offered, unprompted, to put a small card about the shelf beside the till in her café, and Mira accepted with gratitude. She added a line to the book asking people whether they had seen it there, and in two weeks, five new borrowers said that they had. A card that cost almost nothing, placed with someone the neighbourhood trusted, had done better than the printed leaflets.

Mira wrote the lesson of the month in her notebook in a single and very clear line. Word of mouth is free, powerful and impossible to purchase, but it can be earned by making the shelf so useful and so pleasant that people feel moved to mention it. She also resolved to measure the cost of any new way of finding people before she spent more on it.

By the second month the paper book was crowded and creased, and Mira spent her evenings copying names and dates into a notebook that could scarcely keep up. For the first time there was a genuine reason for software, and it was a reason that she had earned rather than imagined. She telephoned Lucas that same night and told him that the moment had come.

Mira checked her notes for what people truly needed, and one request stood out above all the others. Customers kept telephoning the shop to ask whether a particular tool was on the shelf or out on loan, and each call interrupted Mr Reyes in the middle of serving someone else. The need was small, specific and constant, and it was exactly the sort of thing software does well.

Lucas agreed to build only the one thing that the tests had shown to be needed, which was a single plain page listing every tool on the shelf with a clear sign for whether it was in or out. He drew the whole thing on a whiteboard in less than two minutes, humming quietly while he worked. It looked almost insultingly simple to a person of his talents, and Mira found it quite beautiful.

Lucas, who loved his craft, could not resist suggesting additions, and he reeled off a list of maps, ratings, photographs and personalised reminders. Mira felt the old temptation tug at her, since all of it had once been in her notebook, but she shook her head. No test had shown that anybody wanted any of those things, and she did not intend to pay for a guess.

Mira started a page in her notebook headed not yet, and she promised that every feature anyone proposed would go on it, however clever or exciting. An idea on the list was neither rejected nor forgotten, merely held until a small test proved that real people wanted it. The page gave her a kind way of saying no, and it let her friends keep their enthusiasm.

A week later Lucas showed her the first version on his laptop, and it was as plain as a wooden spoon. There was no decoration and nothing clever, but it loaded quickly and its marks were always correct, because he had spent his time on exactly that. The aim, as Mira reminded them both, was a good test and not a careless product.

Mira tried the page on a battered old phone and then showed it to several neighbours, to find out whether anyone could be confused by it. Tomas, who still refused to own a smartphone, would simply telephone the shop as he always had, and the paper book remained beside the shelf as a faithful back-up. She smiled to herself, recalling how confidently she had once assumed that everyone loved tapping a screen.

Within a fortnight the new page was in daily use, and the effect on the shop was easy to measure. The telephone calls asking whether a tool was available fell from about twenty a week to about five, and Mr Reyes, who disliked being interrupted at the till, was delighted. A single, humble page had solved a single, real problem, and that was all that it had been asked to do.

One afternoon a borrower returned a saw with a snapped blade, red-faced and apologising before he had even reached the counter. Mira thanked him for his honesty, and she did not treat the accident as a disaster but as a lesson, because every lending service must decide what happens when something breaks. She then wrote a simple rule: normal wear is covered by the shelf, accidents reported honestly cost nothing, and careless damage is repaired by the borrower.

Every Friday afternoon, Mira, Mr Reyes, Lucas and Kofi met in the back room of the shop and looked together at the same simple numbers on a noticeboard. Nobody was allowed to keep a flattering figure to themselves or to bury an unwelcome one, because bad news that is hidden has a way of growing. Their little weekly meetings were always short, honest and, to everyone's considerable surprise, rather enjoyable.

Mira laid her original sketch, with its glowing map and its star ratings, beside a photograph of the plain pine shelf in Mr Reyes's shop. The first had been beautiful and wrong, and the second was humble and useful, and the difference was that she had stopped loving the solution. What she now cared about was the problem itself, and that, she realised, was what had allowed her to change her mind.

One evening, over tea on the workshop step, Kofi put to her a final and rather daunting question. If Toolshelf were to fail, he wondered, would she still care about the problem it was trying to solve? Mira deliberated for a long while and then replied that she would, because it was the problem and not the product that had taken hold of her, and a stubborn problem can always be attacked from more than one angle.

Mira chose a review date three months ahead, circled it on the calendar and told everyone about it. On that day she and the team would look honestly at the numbers and decide whether to carry on, change course or stop, and nobody was to argue with the schedule when the time came. Knowing in advance when to stop is part of the discipline, she had decided, because few people stop at exactly the right moment by instinct alone.

Jonas, who ran a van full of big machines for hire, came to the shop one morning and watched the shelf for a long time with his arms folded. Mira, instead of feeling threatened, walked over and asked him what he had learned about what people rented and what they merely wished to rent. He answered at length, and she went home with a new note for the not-yet list.

Hana, who owned a small paint shop on Birch Road, heard about the shelf from a customer and asked whether she could have one too. Mira did not take it as proof of anything, but as the next small test, and she wrote a target for one month on the new street before agreeing. If it worked on Birch Road as well, then she would know that it was not simply a happy accident of Alder Street.

A year later, in this imagined story, Toolshelf stood on shelves in three shops, in Mr Reyes's hardware store, in Hana's paint shop and in a bicycle shop on Mill Lane. Some four hundred people had joined, and every part of the service had been built because a small test had shown it was wanted. It had grown slowly, and the slow growth had been the secret of keeping it honest.

On the shelf in Mr Reyes's shop sat the very drill that Mira had once bought for a single job, and it now went out almost every week to a neighbour who needed it. Its label had grown soft at the edges from handling, and the case showed the marks of a dozen different hands. She thought, with a private smile, that it was the most satisfied drill on the whole of Alder Street.

Mira slowly realised that the method she had stumbled upon was not restricted to ventures or shops. The same cycle of guess, test, count and decide could be applied to starting a club, perfecting a recipe, trying a new job or planning a project at home. Anywhere there was an idea and a risk of being wrong, a small and honest experiment could save a great deal of time and heartache.

Even Kofi, who had been sceptical of anything that smelled of business theory, borrowed the method for a new chair of his own design. Before he cut a single board, he showed a drawing to three customers and asked them about the last chair they had bought and why they had chosen it. Their answers changed the design, and he admitted, grudgingly, that it had saved him a month of wasted wood.

In the end, the whole method fits into a handful of steps: list your guesses, find the riskiest, test it as cheaply as you can, count what people actually do, and decide what to do next. Do this again and again, and your ideas will meet reality early, when it is still gentle. This book is general information only, written to help you think, and it is not financial advice.
